## Geometry and distances

Collision primitives are convex: spheres, boxes, cylinders, capsules and
convex hulls of points. Each is represented internally as a core shape plus a
radius, so a capsule is a segment swept by a sphere.

`geom_distance()` returns the separation distance and witness points. Sphere
and capsule pairs use closed-form segment distances (exact depth when they
overlap). Other pairs use the Gilbert, Johnson and Keerthi (GJK) algorithm on
support functions. When the cores of a GJK pair overlap, the expanding
polytope algorithm (EPA) grows a polytope inside the Minkowski difference
$A - B$ until its face nearest the origin is part of the boundary; the
distance to that face is the penetration depth, the length of the shortest
translation that separates the shapes.

EPA keeps two bounds on the depth: the nearest face of the polytope (a lower
bound) and the smallest support value seen along a face normal (an upper
bound). It stops when they agree to about $10^{-9}$ of the object size, and
`depth_known` is then `TRUE`. Curved cores in symmetric positions can exhaust
the iteration budget first. Two identical coaxial cylinders are the classic
case, because every radial direction is equally deep. `depth_known` is then
`FALSE`, `distance` is the shallower estimate and `distance_bounds` brackets
the true value. The yes/no collision answer is exact in both cases.

```{r}
geom_distance(geom_sphere(0.5), geom_sphere(0.3), robot_pose(), transl(2, 0, 0))$distance
d <- geom_distance(geom_box(c(1, 1, 1)), geom_sphere(0.2), robot_pose(), transl(1.5, 1.5, 0))
c(d$distance, sqrt(2) - 0.2)
d$point_a
geom_distance(geom_box(c(1, 1, 1)), geom_box(c(1, 1, 1)), robot_pose(), transl(0.5, 0, 0))$distance
# Two unit cubes, one turned 45 degrees: depth 0.5 + sqrt(2) / 2 - 0.9.
geom_distance(geom_box(c(1, 1, 1)), geom_box(c(1, 1, 1)), robot_pose(),
              robot_pose(rotz(pi / 4), c(0.9, 0, 0)))$distance
0.9 - 0.5 - sqrt(2) / 2
cyl <- geom_distance(geom_cylinder(0.5, 10), geom_cylinder(0.5, 10))
cyl[c("depth_known", "distance", "distance_bounds")]
```

Mesh geometry from URDF files is kept for reference but is not collidable.

## Robots in an environment

Attach geometry to links with `robot_attach_geometry()`, or wrap every DH
link in a capsule with `robot_capsule_links()`. Obstacles are geometries with
world poses.

```{r}
arm <- robot_capsule_links(robot_example("planar2"), radius = 0.05)
env <- robot_environment(
  block = geom_box(c(0.4, 0.4, 0.4), origin = transl(1.5, 0, 0)),
  post = geom_cylinder(0.1, 1, origin = transl(-1, 1, 0))
)
robot_check_collision(arm, c(0, 0), env)
robot_check_collision(arm, c(pi / 2, 0), env, distances = TRUE)
```

Self-collision checks skip links that share a joint (they always touch at the
joint) and any pairs listed in `ignore_pairs`.

```{r}
arm3 <- robot_capsule_links(robot_example("planar3"), 0.05)
robot_check_collision(arm3, c(0, 3, 3))$in_collision
```

### Paths and the resolution caveat

`robot_check_path()` interpolates each segment in joint space with steps no
larger than `resolution` and checks every sample. Both endpoints below are
free, yet the straight joint space path sweeps through the block:

```{r}
res <- robot_check_path(arm, rbind(c(pi / 2, 0), c(-pi / 2, 0)), env)
res$valid
res$q
```

This is a discrete check. A thin obstacle can slip between samples if the
resolution is coarse relative to the obstacle size and the link lengths.

### Continuous checking

`method = "continuous"` removes that caveat with conservative advancement.
At the current configuration it computes the clearance $d$ of every geometry
pair and a bound $M$ on how far any point of the pair can move per unit of
the segment parameter. For a revolute joint, a point at distance $r$ from the
joint axis moves at most $r$ per radian, and $r$ is bounded by the fixed
frame offsets of the chain plus the size of the geometry. Moving by $d / M$
cannot cause contact, so the check steps forward by that amount until it
either reaches the end of the segment or a clearance reaches zero. The end
configuration of every segment is then checked with the same contact rule as
`robot_check_collision()`, so a path that ends touching an obstacle is
invalid. Prismatic joints enter the lever arms through the extension they
actually reach on the segment, so the bound holds with
`check_limits = FALSE` and for joints without finite limits.

Here a thin post sits between two samples of a coarse discrete check:

```{r}
post <- robot_environment(post = geom_box(c(0.02, 0.02, 1), origin = transl(cos(0.6), sin(0.6), 0)))
P <- rbind(c(0, 0), c(1.2, 0))
robot_check_path(arm, P, post, resolution = 0.5)$valid
cc <- robot_check_path(arm, P, post, method = "continuous")
cc$valid
cc$q
robot_check_collision(arm, cc$q, post)$min_distance
```

The configuration returned is the first contact along the motion, up to the
tolerance `tol`.

## Sampling-based planners

`robot_planner()` sets up a planner; `robot_plan()` runs it.

| Algorithm | Idea | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `"rrt"` | Grow a tree toward random samples, with goal bias | Fast, paths are jagged |
| `"rrt_connect"` | Two trees that greedily try to meet | Usually fastest for single queries |
| `"rrt_star"` | RRT with rewiring in a shrinking radius | Improves cost as samples increase |
| `"prm"` | Roadmap of random free samples, queried with Dijkstra | Reusable for many queries |

```{r}
planner <- robot_planner(arm, "rrt_connect", env, step_size = 0.3)
plan <- robot_plan(planner, start = c(-0.8, 0), goal = c(0.8, 0), seed = 1)
plan
robot_check_path(arm, plan$path, env, resolution = 0.01)$valid
short <- robot_shortcut(plan, seed = 1)
c(original = plan$length, shortcut = short$length)
```

A failure only means that no path was found within the budget:

```{r}
blocked <- robot_planner(validity = function(q) abs(q[1] - 0.5) > 0.05,
                         bounds = rbind(c(0, 1), c(0, 1)), max_iterations = 200)
robot_plan(blocked, c(0.1, 0.1), c(0.9, 0.1), seed = 1)$message
```

### Planning without a robot model

A `validity` function and `bounds` define any configuration space. This makes
the planners easy to study on 2D examples:

```{r, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 5}
walls <- function(q) {
  !(abs(q[1] - 0.33) < 0.03 && q[2] < 0.7) && !(abs(q[1] - 0.66) < 0.03 && q[2] > 0.3)
}
draw <- function() {
  rect(0.30, 0, 0.36, 0.7, col = "grey70", border = NA)
  rect(0.63, 0.3, 0.69, 1, col = "grey70", border = NA)
}
box <- rbind(c(0, 1), c(0, 1))
for (alg in c("rrt", "rrt_connect", "rrt_star", "prm")) {
  pl <- robot_planner(validity = walls, bounds = box, algorithm = alg,
                      step_size = 0.08, resolution = 0.005,
                      max_iterations = 1500, prm_nodes = 250)
  p <- robot_plan(pl, c(0.1, 0.1), c(0.9, 0.9), seed = 3)
  plot(p, obstacles = draw)
  mtext(sprintf("length %.3f, %d nodes", p$length, p$nodes), side = 3, line = 0.2, cex = 0.8)
}
```

### Practical advice

* Keep `resolution` below the smallest obstacle feature, in joint units.
* Use `seed` for reproducible results; the global random state is restored.
* RRT* converges to optimal paths only as samples grow without bound. Use
  `robot_shortcut()` for a quick improvement of any planner's output.
* Planning runs in R and calls the collision checker many times. Expect
  seconds for 2 to 6 DOF problems with simple geometry.
